context.text: Imagine a town map drawn on a grid, with each square 100 m wide. A straight road runs from the point $A(2, 5)$ to the point $B(8, 5)$. The council wants to put a bus stop exactly halfway along the road. What are the two coordinates of the bus stop?

statements.text: Midpoint C of A(1, 2) and B(5, 6) is found by averaging coordinates: C((1+5)/2, (2+6)/2), i.e. C(3, 4). Formula: $C\left(\frac{1+5}{2}, \frac{2+6}{2}\right)=C(3, 4)$

If A(x1, y1), B(x2, y2), M(x, y) where M is the midpoint of AB, then triangles BEM and MDA are congruent, so AD = ME. Hence x − x1 = x2 − x, so 2x = x1 + x2, x = (x1+x2)/2. Similarly MD = BE gives y − y1 = y2 − y, so 2y = y1 + y2, y = (y1+y2)/2. So M((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2). Formula: $M\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$

context.text: In general, you can deduce the law of the coordinate of the midpoint of a straight segment as follows.

Suppose two friends live at $A(2, 4)$ and $B(8, 10)$ on a map grid, and they agree to meet at the point exactly halfway between their homes. The meeting point is the midpoint of the straight segment $\overline{AB}$. What are the coordinates of the meeting point?

Imagine a map grid where a school is at $A(2, 1)$ and a bakery is at $M(5, 3)$. The bakery is exactly halfway between the school and a sports club at point $B$. What are the coordinates of the sports club $B$?

statements.text: The two ends of the line segment
The two coordinates of the midpoint of a straight segment
